description:
#intel #arc #b580 #gpureview #honestreview 
Intel ARC B580 Founders Edition review and thoughts - dont buy it!

We all hoped that Intel would be the saviour of budget gaming in 2024 and 2025, If we were to believe the marketing and hype that Tom and Steve showed us, there was some great architecture and design in the B580 and on paper it looks like a contender.
192 bit bus PCIe Gen4 X 8 lanes, single 8 pin power, low TDP and 12GB of VRAM, it seemed to be a market busting product with an MSRP of about £260!
The reality is that for a long time the MSRP's where jacked up and the drivers and performance wasn't any better than the older A770 card.
For me with an Intel Core 245K on a Z890 chipset, it could be said that the platform should be right on point for some really thrilling performance, the truth though is that is feels weak, has very inconsistent frametimes and framerates, and you would likely be better off buying an old used RTX3060TI or similar.
I am somewhat disappointed with this card, but hopefully the drivers and optimisation can turn this around, but will it be to late for the Intel ARC team?

B580 is not good for 1080p, at all. Lower resolutions make the frame pacing problems even worse. Arc in general is only good if someone wants to run 1440p or 4k for cheap, because it actually catches up to other cards in its price class in those resolutions.

Said another way, only get Arc products if you are generally happy at 50-80 FPS. Do not get Arc if you expect to be able to push over 100 FPS, as the drivers and bad frame pacing make 100+ FPS feel worse than it should.

comments.text:
Thanks for the thoughtful review, Mike. I bought an Asrock B580 Challenger for $330 in May. Here in South Africa, it was the best option at the time. Stuttering depends on the game but does occur, perhaps moreso in DX11 titles.

Chips and Cheese did an analysis and found that the driver is working in a different, possibly suboptimal way compared to AMD. comments.text: If ever a company was the poster child for "you can't have it both ways" it's Intel. The GPU is a different beast to most other components in that drivers need regular and meaningful updates. Supporting a product goes a bit further than (eventually) making sure it's available at MSRP. There is clearly turmoil within the company about the lower margins because of the relatively larger die size. This may be true but the additional costs for driver support still need to be borne. Those costs are miniscule compared to what the product originally cost to develop. If they are not met then what was the point in the first place ? I think it was Moores Law that first highlighted the inconsistent support and muddled thinking prior to launch. I don't think much has changed.  Here comes the new boss same as the old boss a certain group used to sing.
